0.1 What this handbook is

This is the single procedure every employee follows to take an automation project from an idea to a working system in a customer's hands, and then keep it working. You do not need to know everything before you start. You need to follow the stages in order, finish every checklist, and get every sign-off.

If you are ever unsure what to do next, open this book at the stage your project is in. The answer is there. If it is not, ask your Technical Lead and then tell the Founder so the book can be fixed.

0.2 How to use it

  1. Find your project's current stage in the Stage Map (section 0.4).
  2. Read that stage file once completely before you start doing anything.
  3. Do the numbered steps in order. Tick the Done checklist as you go.
  4. Save every deliverable in the exact folder named in the stage.
  5. Ask for the gate sign-off. You may not start the next stage without it.
  6. Update the project status sheet every Friday.

0.3 The ten golden rules

  1. Never skip a stage or a gate. Skipping is how projects fail.
  2. Understand the customer's work before writing code. Code written for a misunderstood process is waste.
  3. Choose the simplest solution that works. Use AI only where rules cannot do the job.
  4. Never trust AI output blindly. Every AI answer is checked by rules before it is used.
  5. Never put a password, API key or customer data into Git. Not once, not "temporarily".
  6. Write the test before or with the code. No test, no merge.
  7. Small steps, saved often. Commit at least every time something works.
  8. Write it down. If it is not in a document or a ticket, it did not happen.
  9. Ask early. Being stuck for 30 minutes without asking is a mistake, not a virtue.
  10. Customer data belongs to the customer. Treat it as if it were your own bank details.

0.5 Who is who (plain words)

Role What they really do You ask them when
Founder Decides what we sell, signs contracts and prices You need a decision about money, scope or customers
Project Manager (PM) Plans the work, tracks time, talks to the customer daily You need priorities, deadlines or customer contacts

0.6 Words you will hear every day (glossary)

Term Meaning in one line
Automation A computer doing a repeated task so a person does not have to
Workflow The ordered steps from a trigger to a result
Trigger The event that starts a workflow (a new email, a file, 9 a.m.)
API A doorway one program offers so another program can ask it for things
Webhook A message another system sends to us when something happens
JSON A plain-text way of writing structured data, like {"total": 11800}
Schema The agreed shape of data: which fields, which types
Database Organised storage for data that survives restarts
LLM Large language model; the AI that reads and writes text
Prompt The instructions we give the AI
Token A piece of text the AI is charged by, roughly ¾ of a word
OCR Turning a picture of text into real text
RAG Giving the AI our documents to look things up before answering
Agent An AI that chooses its own next steps using tools; use rarely
Repository (repo) The folder of project code tracked by Git
Git The tool that records every change to the code and who made it
Commit One saved, described change in Git
Branch A separate line of work so your changes do not break others
Pull request (PR) A request to merge your branch after someone reviews it
CI/CD Robots that automatically test (CI) and deploy (CD) your code
Environment A separate copy of the system: local, staging, production
Staging The safe practice copy of the live system
Production The real, live system the customer uses
Secret A password, key or token that must never be shared or committed
Idempotency Doing the same request twice has the same effect as once (no double posting)
Gate A mandatory approval point between stages
Scope Exactly what we promised to build, no more, no less
Change request (CR) A written, priced request to change the agreed scope
SLA The service level we promise (response times, uptime)
UAT User acceptance testing: the customer tries it and signs off
MRR Monthly recurring revenue: subscription income each month
Margin Revenue minus cost, as a share of revenue
Technical debt Shortcuts taken now that will cost time later

0.7 How to read the stage files

Every stage file has the same sections, in the same order:

  1. Purpose — why this stage exists.
  2. Who and when — owner, approver, time.
  3. Before you start — what you must already have.
  4. Step by step — numbered actions.
  5. Worked example — the same stage done for our sample project (GST purchase-bill automation).
  6. Deliverables — files you must produce and where they go.
  7. Done checklist — tick every box.
  8. Common mistakes — what beginners get wrong.
  9. Gate sign-off — who approves and what they check.

0.8 The running example

Throughout the book we follow one sample project so you can see every stage done once:

Customer: a 6-person chartered-accountant (CA) firm with 40 small-business clients. Problem: staff type about 1,500 supplier bills a month into accounting software by hand, taking about 6 minutes each, with typing errors. Solution: a system that reads each bill, checks the GST rules, sends doubtful bills to a person, and posts good ones to the accounting software.

A small working version of the rule-checking part is in reference-project/. You will build and run it in Stage 7.

Part 1 — How a Software Company Really Works

Read this before Stage 0. It explains the world you are joining: the people, the paperwork, the rhythm of the week, and why each rule exists.

1.1 The big picture: how money and work flow

Customer has a problem
      ↓
Sales/Founder talks to customer  →  Proposal and price approved
      ↓
Contract (SOW) signed  →  Project created, Project ID issued
      ↓
Analysis → Design → Build → Test → Deploy      (this handbook)
      ↓
Customer accepts (UAT sign-off)  →  Invoice raised
      ↓
Support and maintenance  →  Monthly subscription or retainer = recurring revenue

A software company earns money only when the customer's problem is solved and the customer says so. Everything in this handbook exists to make that happen reliably and profitably.

1.2 Why companies use stages and gates

Building the wrong thing is the most expensive mistake. Finding a misunderstanding in Stage 2 costs an hour of talking. Finding it in Stage 13 costs weeks of rebuilding. Gates are cheap checks placed where mistakes are cheapest to catch.

1.3 The organisation, department by department

Department Purpose Typical outputs
Management Direction, money, hiring, contracts Budgets, priorities, approvals
Sales and Business Development Find and win customers Proposals, demos, signed contracts
Business Analysis Understand the customer's process Process maps, requirements
Engineering Build the product Code, workflows, APIs
AI and Data Make AI steps reliable Prompts, evaluation reports
QA (Quality Assurance) Find faults before customers do Test plans, bug reports
DevOps and Infrastructure Run software safely Servers, deployment, monitoring
Security Protect data and systems Reviews, policies
Customer Success and Support Keep customers happy and productive Training, tickets, health checks
Finance and Admin Invoices, tax, payroll, compliance Invoices, books, filings

1.4 Tickets: how work is tracked

Every piece of work is a ticket (also called a task or issue) on a shared board. No ticket, no work.

A good ticket has: title (verb first: "Validate GSTIN check character"), description (what and why), acceptance criteria (how we know it is done), estimate (hours), assignee, priority, project ID.

Board columns, left to right: Backlog → Ready → In Progress → In Review → Testing → Done.

  • Ready means the ticket is clear enough to start (Definition of Ready: has acceptance criteria and an estimate).
  • Done means finished to the team's standard (Definition of Done, section 1.9).

1.5 The weekly rhythm

When What Length Purpose
Every morning Stand-up 10–15 min Each person says: done yesterday, doing today, blocked by
Monday Sprint or week planning 30–60 min Pick the tickets for this week
Daily Customer update by PM short Customer is never surprised
Wednesday Technical review 30 min Design questions, code problems
Friday Status report + demo to team 30 min Show what works; update status sheet
Monthly Cost and quality review 60 min Check money, errors, customer health
Quarterly Security and backup-restore drill half day Prove we can recover

Stand-up rule: it is a status check, not a discussion. Long topics go to a separate meeting.

1.6 How code travels from your laptop to the customer

Your laptop (local)  →  Git branch  →  Pull request  →  Automatic tests (CI)
      →  Code review by Technical Lead  →  Merge to main
      →  Staging server (practice copy)  →  QA and customer test
      →  Approval  →  Production server (live)  →  Monitoring

Rules of this path:

  • Nobody edits the live system directly. Ever.
  • Nobody pushes straight to main. All changes go through a pull request and review.
  • Staging first. Production gets only what already worked on staging.
  • Every release has a version number and a rollback plan (how to go back if it goes wrong).

1.7 The three environments

Environment Used by Data Secrets
Local (your laptop) You Fake/sample only Your own test keys in .env (never committed)
Staging Team, QA, customer demo Fake or customer-authorised test data Staging keys
Production The customer's staff Real customer data Production keys held in a secret manager, few people can see them

A mistake on local costs nothing. A mistake on production costs trust. That is why they are separate.

1.8 Documents a company keeps (and who writes them)

Document Written by Read by Why it exists
Market/opportunity report Analyst Founder Decide whether to pursue
Process document (AS-IS/TO-BE) Business Analyst Everyone Shared understanding of the work
Requirements and scope freeze BA + PM Customer, team What we promised
Architecture document Technical Lead Engineers How it is built
Test plan and report QA PM, customer Proof of quality
Security review Security Founder Proof it is safe enough
Cost and price sheet Founder + PM Management Profit control
Runbook DevOps Support How to fix common problems
User and admin manuals Customer Success Customer How to use and manage it
Status report PM Everyone Weekly truth
Change request PM Customer, Founder Controlled scope changes

If a decision is only in a chat message, treat it as not decided. Put it in the project folder.

1.9 Definition of Done (for any ticket)

A ticket is Done only when all are true:

  • The code or document does what the acceptance criteria say.
  • Automated tests exist for it and pass.
  • A second person has reviewed it.
  • Documentation is updated (README, comments for public functions, this ticket).
  • No secrets or customer data are in the change.
  • It has run successfully on staging (for deployable work).
  • The ticket links to the commit or pull request.

1.10 Code review: what it is and why

Code review means a colleague reads your change before it is merged. It catches bugs, spreads knowledge, and keeps quality consistent. It is not criticism of you. Rules:

  • Keep pull requests small (under about 300 changed lines).
  • Write a clear description: what, why, how to test.
  • Respond to every comment: fix it or explain.
  • Reviewers check the list in Appendix C.

1.11 Bugs and severity

Severity Meaning Example Reaction
P1 Critical Wrong data posted or system down for everyone Bills posted twice Drop everything; tell PM and Founder at once
P2 Major One feature broken, workaround exists Reviewer screen will not load for one client Fix within the agreed support time
P3 Minor Small defect or cosmetic Misspelt label Schedule in normal work

1.12 Customer communication rules

  • The PM is the customer's main contact. Engineers do not promise dates or features directly.
  • Never say "yes, we can add that" in a call. Say "I will note it and our Project Manager will come back with effort and cost." That is how scope creep is controlled.
  • Be honest about problems early, with a plan.
  • Never ask for or accept customer passwords by chat or email. Use the agreed secure method.

1.13 Professional habits that matter more than talent

  • Name files and branches clearly (Appendix A).
  • Keep your work visible: update tickets daily.
  • Test your own work before asking for review.
  • Write small, readable code; comments explain why, not what.
  • Say "I do not know yet" and then find out.
  • Protect confidentiality: customer names, data and prices stay inside the company.

1.14 How a project earns profit (and how it loses it)

Profit comes from: accurate estimates, frozen scope, reuse of components, low support load, and good customer fit. Profit disappears through: scope creep without change requests, unplanned rework, wrong customers, too much support, and unverified prices. Every rule in this handbook protects one of those.

Part 2 — The Folder Structure, Explained

A tidy folder structure is how a team finds things without asking. Every project at VEL uses the same structure, so you can open any project and know where everything is. There are two levels: the company drive (documents, contracts, research) and the project repository (code).

2.1 Level 1 — Company drive (documents)

VEL-Company/
├── 01-Management/            policies, budgets, hiring, templates owned by the Founder
├── 02-Sales-and-Customers/
│   ├── Leads/                one file per prospect
│   └── Customers/
│       └── <Customer-Name>/
│           ├── contracts/    SOW, agreement, DPA (signed copies only)
│           ├── meetings/     notes, dated YYYY-MM-DD
│           └── onboarding/
├── 03-Research/              market reports, competitor notes, interview recordings
├── 04-Projects/
│   └── P-2026-001_GST-Bill-Automation/     one folder per project, named with Project ID
│       ├── 00-admin/         project.yaml, status reports, risk register, change requests, gate sign-offs
│       ├── 01-discovery/     interviews, opportunity score
│       ├── 02-analysis/      process sheet, AS-IS, TO-BE, bottleneck analysis
│       ├── 03-requirements/  scope freeze, input/output spec, acceptance criteria
│       ├── 04-design/        architecture, data model, UI mockups, agent spec
│       ├── 05-testing/       test plan, evaluation set descriptions, reports
│       ├── 06-security/      checklist, test evidence
│       ├── 07-commercial/    cost sheet, price sheet, proposal, ROI report
│       ├── 08-deployment/    readiness checklist, runbook, release notes
│       └── 09-handover/      manuals, training material, acceptance sign-off

├── 06-Finance/               invoices, expenses (Founder and accounts only)
└── 07-Training/              this handbook, videos, onboarding material

Rules

  • One project, one folder, named P-<year>-<number>_<Short-Name>.
  • Copy a template; never edit the master.
  • Files are named YYYY-MM-DD_description_vN.ext, e.g. 2026-11-03_process-sheet_v2.docx.
  • Signed or final documents are read-only; changes create a new version.
  • Customer data files are never stored here unless the contract allows it and the folder is access-restricted.

What each part is for, in plain words

Folder / file Think of it as Beginner tip
README.md The front door If a stranger cannot run the project from it, fix it
.gitignore A "do not photograph" list Add .env and __pycache__/ before your first commit
.env.example A blank form of settings Copy to .env, fill with your own test values

2.3 Naming conventions

Thing Rule Example
Project ID P-<year>-<3 digits> P-2026-001
Repository lowercase, hyphens gst-bill-automation
Branch type/ticket-short-name feature/GBA-12-gstin-check
Commit message <Ticket>: <what changed> GBA-12: add GSTIN check-character validation

2.4 What must never be in the repository

  • Passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates, .env files.
  • Real customer data, real invoices, real GSTINs of customers.
  • Large generated files, virtual environments, node_modules.
  • Personal notes and screenshots with customer information.

If you commit one by mistake: stop, tell the Technical Lead immediately. The secret must be revoked and replaced even if you delete the file, because Git remembers history.

Branch Meaning Who can change it
